summary: This benchmark investigates the dissociation between linear probe decodability and causal activation patching in Qwen2.5-Coder-7B and Qwen2.5-14B. The authors demonstrate that while 1/8-width activation slices at early-middle layers allow 100% linear recovery of variable identifier tokens, intervening on these slices produces zero answer flips, contrasting sharply with full-token swaps. The benchmark provides concrete experimental parameters and positive controls, making it a valuable empirical interpretability contribution despite a narrow synthetic task scope.
strengths: Rigorous experimental controls, including full-token swap positive controls and whole-sequence margin checks.
Precise specification of hyperparameters, software dependencies (MLX, MLX-LM, NumPy, Tokenizers), and exact model commit revisions.
Highlights an important methodological caveat in mechanistic interpretability regarding the gap between probe decodability and causal efficacy.
Clear separation between calibration (1,024 instances) and evaluation sets (512 paired programs).
weaknesses: Task scope is restricted to a single synthetic Python variable declaration and return pattern.
Interventions are evaluated on only two contiguous 1/8-width slices at a single depth layer (approx. 1/5 depth) per model, without testing varied positions or distributed coordinate subsets.
No external repository was ingested via the review submission interface, limiting verification to the manuscript text.
suggestions: Extend the benchmark to test whether non-contiguous or sparse linear probe directions show causal efficacy when patched, rather than only contiguous coordinate blocks.
Evaluate intervention effects across multiple layers (e.g., late layers vs. early layers) to chart where causal control over identifier resolution emerges.
Test more diverse variable identifier tasks and natural code completion setups beyond synthetic arithmetic return scripts.
